lessons.title: Every noun is capitalised — and every noun has a gender
lessons.summary: German writes every noun with a capital letter, and every noun is der, die or das — so learn the article as part of the word.
lessons.rule:
A noun is a word that names something: a thing, a person, a place or an idea — house, coffee, Berlin, work, love. In German every single noun is written with a capital letter, not only at the start of a sentence and not only for names. Ich trinke Kaffee. Kaffee sits in the middle and still gets a big K. This is a gift when you read: the capitals show you instantly which words are the things. Verbs like trinken and describing words like gut stay lowercase.

Now the harder fact. Every German noun belongs to one of three groups, and the group decides which word you use for the: der, die or das. Books call the groups masculine, feminine and neuter, but this has almost nothing to do with male and female. It is just a label attached to the word, like a type on a variable. der Tisch (table), die Lampe (lamp), das Fenster (window) — no table is male, no lamp is female.

The proof everyone quotes: das Mädchen means the girl, and it is neuter. A real girl, a neuter word. So stop trying to guess the article from the meaning. It will not work.

The one habit that saves you months: never learn a noun on its own. Do not learn Haus. Learn das Haus. Say the article out loud every time, put it on the flashcard, write it in your notes. A noun without its article is half a word — in a few lessons der turns into den and dem, and you cannot do that if you never knew it was der in the first place.

Good news for the next lesson: the ending of a noun predicts the article about 80% of the time. Anything ending in -ung is die; anything ending in -chen is das. Turkish has no articles and no gender at all, so for a while this feels like pure extra work with no payoff. It does pay off — every case, every adjective ending and half of German word order hangs off it.

lessons.title: Predicting der / die / das from the ending
lessons.summary: The last few letters of a noun give away its article about 80% of the time — around twenty patterns instead of hundreds of separate facts.
lessons.rule:
Lesson 1 left you with a scary picture: hundreds of nouns, three articles, no logic. Here is the fix. The ending of a word — its last two or three letters — tells you the article roughly 80% of the time. About twenty patterns replace hundreds of separate memories.

The three tables below are the core, and the die list is the strongest of all. -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion and -tät have essentially no exceptions. If a word ends in -ung, it is die. Every time.

Meaning helps too, but only in a few tight groups:

  • der — male people (der Vater, der Bruder), days (der Montag), months (der Mai), seasons (der Sommer) and weather words (der Regen, der Wind, der Schnee)
  • die — female people (die Mutter, die Schwester), most flowers and trees (die Rose, die Blume) and numbers used as words (die Eins, die Drei)
  • das — young beings (das Kind, das Baby), metals (das Gold, das Silber) and single letters (das A, das B)

One extra pattern is worth as much as the tables: nouns ending in -e are feminine about 90% of the time — die Lampe, die Straße, die Blume, die Schule, die Sprache. The ones to watch are der Junge (boy), der Name and das Auge (eye).

When the ending and the meaning disagree, the ending wins. das Mädchen is a girl but ends in -chen, so it is neuter — every -chen and -lein word is, because those endings mean little. And be honest about -er: it only means der when the word is a doer — der Lehrer (teacher), der Fahrer (driver), der Computer. Plain things break it: das Fenster, das Wasser, das Messer, die Mutter, die Schwester.

examples.note: -ung is always die. This is the one pattern with no exceptions worth worrying about.
-ent gives you der, like -er, -or and -ling.
The ending beats the meaning: -chen makes it das, even for a real girl.

examples.de: Die Bäckerei öffnet um sechs Uhr.
examples.en: The bakery opens at six o'clock.
examples.note: -ei is die. You will read this word on every second corner in Germany.
It ends in -er but it is das. The -er rule only works for people and machines that do something.
All four seasons are der: der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter.

mistakes.why: -chen means little and always makes the word neuter. The ending decides, never the person.
-ung is feminine without exception, so any word ending in -ung is die.
-in marks a female person and is always die, even though the base word der Lehrer is masculine.
-er only predicts der for doers like der Fahrer. Everyday objects such as Fenster, Wasser and Messer are neuter.

drills.question: ___ Wohnung ist neu.
drills.explain: Every noun ending in -ung is feminine, so it takes die.

drills.question: ___ Mädchen heißt Lena.
drills.explain: -chen makes a word neuter whatever it means, and the ending always beats the meaning.

drills.question: Wo ist ___ Zeitung? (der / die / das)
drills.explain: Zeitung ends in -ung, and that ending is feminine every single time.

drills.question: Ist ___ Gemüse frisch? (der / die / das)
drills.explain: Nouns that start with Ge- are usually neuter, like das Geschenk and das Geschäft.

drills.question: Which one is correct?
drills.explain: Words ending in -um came from Latin and are neuter, like das Zentrum and das Datum.
The -in ending makes the female job title feminine, so it is die even though der Lehrer is masculine.

drills.question: ___ Fenster ist kaputt.
drills.explain: -er only means der for doers such as der Fahrer; plain objects like Fenster and Messer are neuter.

drills.answer: Der Student lernt jeden Tag Deutsch
drills.explain: -ent gives der, and the verb lernt stays in second position no matter how long the sentence gets.

lessons.title: Making nouns plural — the five patterns
lessons.summary: Five plural endings, often plus an umlaut — and one genuine relief: in the plural the article is always die.
lessons.rule:
Plural simply means more than one: one house, two houses. English adds -s and is finished. German has five different endings, and often changes the vowel on top of that.

First the relief, and it is a big one: in the plural the article is always die. der Mann becomes die Männer. das Kind becomes die Kinder. die Frau becomes die Frauen. All three genders collapse into one. Gender only exists in the singular — so if you are unsure of an article and the word is plural, you are safe.

The five endings are -e, -er, -(e)n, -s and nothing at all. Very often the vowel also takes an umlaut — the two dots in ä ö ü, which change how the vowel sounds: a becomes ä (Mann, Männer), u becomes ü (Stuhl, Stühle), o becomes ö (Sohn, Söhne). Only a, o and u can take the dots.

There are tendencies you can lean on. Feminine nouns almost always take -(e)n and never take an umlaut. Masculine nouns usually take -e, often with an umlaut. Neuter nouns take -e or -er. Anything borrowed from English or French takes -s: die Autos, die Handys, die Hotels. And nouns that already end in -er, -en or -el usually add nothing at all, so the plural looks exactly like the singular: das Fenster and die Fenster.

These are tendencies, not laws — so do the same thing you did with the article: learn the plural as part of the word. Not Haus, not even das Haus, but das Haus, die Häuser. Two extra seconds now instead of guessing forever. One last trap from Turkish: Turkish says üç ev, literally three house, keeping the noun singular after a number. German never does that. After a number the noun must be plural: drei Häuser.

tables.title: The plural article is always die
Which gender usually takes which plural

examples.note: das Kind becomes die Kinder — the -er group, and the article changes to die.
der Stuhl becomes die Stühle: the ending -e plus an umlaut, u to ü.
Auto came from another language, so it takes -s, just like in English.
das Fenster becomes die Fenster — no ending at all. Only the article die tells you there is more than one.
A few words only exist in the plural: die Eltern (parents), die Leute (people), die Ferien (holidays).

mistakes.why: In the plural every noun takes die, whatever its article was in the singular.
Turkish leaves the noun singular after a number (üç ev). German always marks the plural, even when the number already says how many.
-s only belongs to foreign words like Auto and Handy. Most German nouns use -e, -er or -(e)n instead.
Nouns already ending in -er, -en or -el usually add nothing, so singular and plural look identical.

drills.explain: Every plural noun takes die, so the singular gender no longer matters.

drills.question: der Stuhl → ?
drills.explain: Masculine nouns commonly add -e and change the vowel to an umlaut at the same time.

drills.question: Ich habe zwei ___. (das Kind)
drills.explain: German must show the plural on the noun after a number, unlike Turkish.

drills.question: Wir haben drei ___. (das Auto)
drills.explain: Auto is a borrowed word, and borrowed words take -s.

drills.question: das Fenster → ?
drills.explain: Nouns ending in -er usually add nothing, so only the article shows that it is plural.

drills.answer: Die Häuser in Berlin sind teuer
drills.explain: das Haus takes -er plus an umlaut, and every plural noun switches to the article die.

drills.question: die Lampe → ?
drills.explain: Feminine nouns almost always add -n or -en and never take an umlaut.

drills.answer: Meine zwei Schwestern wohnen in Hamburg
drills.explain: die Schwester adds -n in the plural, and the verb still stands in second position.

lessons.title: der/die/das and ein/eine — "the" and "a"
lessons.summary: German never lets a noun stand alone: it needs "the" or "a" in front — except in the plural, where "a" simply does not exist.
lessons.rule:
Turkish has no word for the and no word for a. German has six of them, and you cannot leave them out. Almost every German noun walks around with one of these little words in front of it.

Every noun has a gender. This is not about male and female in any real sense — it is a label glued to the word, and you learn it together with the word. Masculine nouns take der, feminine nouns take die, neuter nouns take das. So never learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.

der/die/das means "the" — the one we both already know about. ein/eine means "a" — any one of them, or one you are mentioning for the first time. Da ist ein Café. (you don't know it yet) becomes Das Café ist neu. (now you do).

Two traps for you. First: eine is only for feminine nouns. Masculine and neuter both use plain ein — ein Mann, ein Kind. Second, and bigger: ein has no plural form at all. There is no "eine Bücher". The plural of ein Buch is simply Bücher, with nothing in front of it.

The plural is the one easy part of the whole system: every plural noun takes die as its "the", whatever gender it had in the singular. der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder, die Lampe → die Lampen.

tables.title: Same noun: first mention, then after that

examples.de: Da ist ein Café. Das Café ist neu.
examples.en: There's a café. The café is new.
examples.note: First mention → ein. Second mention, we both know which one → das.
Frage is feminine, so it gets eine. You will say this sentence a lot at work.

examples.de: Der Mann dort ist mein Nachbar.
examples.en: The man over there is my neighbour.
examples.note: Mann is masculine → der. "dort" shows we mean one specific man, so it's definite.
Plural with no article at all. "eine Äpfel" does not exist in German.
Every plural takes die, even though the singular is das Buch.

mistakes.why: Auto is neuter (das Auto), and neuter takes plain ein. Only feminine nouns get eine.
ein/eine has no plural form. In the plural you use no article at all.
Turkish has no articles, so dropping them feels natural. In German a countable noun almost always needs der/die/das or ein/eine in front of it.
Gender belongs to the word, not to the object. You have to memorise Handy together with das.

drills.question: ___ Mann ist mein Nachbar.
drills.explain: Mann is a masculine noun, and masculine "the" is der.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Frage.
drills.explain: Frage is feminine, and feminine is the only gender that takes eine.

drills.question: Das ist ___ Auto. (a — das Auto)
drills.explain: Neuter uses the same short form as masculine, so it is ein and never eine.
The article sits directly in front of its noun, and the verb takes second position.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: There is no plural of ein, so a plural noun mentioned for the first time gets nothing in front of it.

drills.question: Da ist ein Café. ___ Café ist neu. (the)
drills.explain: On the second mention we both know which café, so it switches from ein to the definite article.

drills.question: ___ Bücher sind teuer.
drills.explain: All plurals take die, no matter what the singular gender was.

drills.answer: Ich suche eine Wohnung in Berlin
drills.explain: Wohnung is feminine and you have not named a specific one yet, so it is eine.

lessons.title: Saying no: kein vs nicht
lessons.summary: German has two words for "not": kein cancels a noun, nicht cancels everything else — and nicht has its own place in the sentence.
lessons.rule:
In Turkish you glue the negative onto the verb (gelmiyorum) or add değil. German makes you pick between two different words: kein and nicht. Picking the wrong one is the single most common beginner mistake there is.

kein cancels a noun. A noun is a thing-word: Auto, Zeit, Geld, Hunger. Here is the test: look at what stands in front of the noun. If it is ein/eine, or if there is nothing there, use kein. Ich habe ein Auto → Ich habe kein Auto. Ich habe Zeit → Ich habe keine Zeit. kein takes exactly the same endings as ein.

nicht cancels everything else — verbs (Ich fahre nicht), adjectives, which are describing words like teuer or müde (nicht teuer), places (nicht in Berlin), names (Das ist nicht Emre), and any noun that already has der/die/das or mein/dein in front of it. That slot is taken, so kein cannot get in.

Where does nicht stand? Directly in front of whatever it is aiming at: before an adjective, before a place, before a second verb at the end of the sentence. If there is nothing to aim at, it drops to the very end: Ich arbeite heute nicht. It never goes between the subject and the verb.

One thing early, because you will need it every day: when the noun is the thing being acted on, masculine kein becomes keinen — Ich habe keinen Hunger. Feminine, neuter and plural stay unchanged. The case lessons will explain why; for now just learn the phrase.

Which word do I use?
headers: What stands in front of the noun
rows: no noun — a verb or adjective

tables.title: Where nicht goes
rows: A second verb at the end

examples.note: You could have said "ein Auto", so the negative word is kein.
Zeit had no article in front of it, and that is still kein territory. Zeit is feminine → keine.
There is no noun to cancel, so nicht falls to the end of the sentence.
nicht stands right in front of the describing word it cancels.
mein already fills the slot in front of the noun, so kein is impossible here.
Hunger is masculine and is the thing being had, so kein takes the extra -en.

mistakes.why: Zeit is a noun with nothing in front of it — exactly the situation kein is made for. This is the most frequent negation error of all.
A noun gets only one word in front of it. mein is already there, so you must negate with nicht.
nicht never squeezes in between the subject and the verb. The verb stays in second position and nicht goes to the end.
When there is a place in the sentence, nicht goes in front of it. Only with nothing to aim at does nicht land at the very end.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Auto.
drills.explain: Auto is a noun that could have taken ein, so it is cancelled with kein — and neuter adds no ending.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Zeit.
drills.explain: A bare noun with no article still belongs to kein, and Zeit is feminine so it takes -e.

drills.question: Das ist ___ mein Handy.
drills.explain: mein is already sitting in front of the noun, which blocks kein completely.

drills.question: Ich arbeite heute ___. (not)
drills.explain: There is no adjective, place or noun to aim at, so nicht goes to the end.
nicht stands immediately before the describing word it cancels, not after it.

drills.question: Danke, ich habe ___ Hunger.
drills.explain: Hunger is masculine and it is the thing being had, which is where kein grows the ending -en.
A place phrase pulls nicht in front of it instead of leaving it at the end.

drills.question: Ich kann heute ___ kommen. (not)
drills.explain: When a second verb waits at the end of the sentence, nicht slots in just before it.

lessons.title: ich, du, er, sie, es — and Sie
lessons.summary: The words for I, you, he, she, it, we and they — plus the du/Sie choice that Germans genuinely notice.
lessons.rule:
A pronoun is a short stand-in word so you don't have to repeat a name. Instead of Emre kommt aus der Türkei you say er kommt aus der Türkei. These are the subject pronouns: the person or thing doing the action.

Careful with es. English says "it" for every object. German does not — it follows the noun's gender instead. Wo ist der Schlüssel? — Er ist hier. Wo ist die Rechnung? — Sie ist hier. Only das-nouns turn into es.

Three different sie. sie = she, sie = they, Sie = formal you. The formal one is always written with a capital S, even in the middle of a sentence. Apart from that, the verb ending tells you which is which: sie wohnt (she), sie wohnen (they), Sie wohnen (you, formal). Spoken aloud, sie wohnen and Sie wohnen sound identical — only the situation tells you.

du or Sie? Turkish has sen and siz, so the idea is familiar, but Germany draws the line harder and keeps it much longer. Sie is the safe default with anyone you don't know: shop staff, waiters, your landlord, the Bürgeramt, a doctor, an older neighbour, a new colleague in a traditional company. du is for friends, family, children, teenagers, students — and most IT teams, where du is normal from the first day.

Do not switch to du on your own. The offer comes from the older or more senior person (Wir können uns duzen or Sag doch du), and then you take it. Using du too early is one of the very few language mistakes Germans really do react to.

you — several people you know well
you — formal, one person or many

rows: A stranger, shop staff, a waiter
Default for anyone you don't know.
An older neighbour in the building

examples.de: Ich heiße Emre und ich komme aus der Türkei.
examples.en: My name is Emre and I come from Turkey.
examples.note: ich is written small in the middle of a sentence, unlike English "I".
To a stranger or an official: capital S, verb ending -en.
The same question to a friend. du has its own verb ending, -st.

examples.de: Wo ist der Schlüssel? — Er ist hier.
examples.en: Where is the key? — It's here.
examples.note: Schlüssel is a der-noun, so it becomes er. German follows gender, not the English "it".
The -t ending shows this is one person: she, not they.
ihr is for two or more people you would each call du — a couple of friends, for example.

mistakes.wrong: Wie heißt du? — to the clerk at the Bürgeramt
mistakes.right: Wie heißen Sie? — to the clerk at the Bürgeramt
mistakes.why: du with a stranger or an official sounds rude in Germany, even when you mean it warmly. Start with Sie every time.

mistakes.wrong: Ich komme aus der Türkei und Ich wohne in Berlin.
mistakes.right: Ich komme aus der Türkei und ich wohne in Berlin.
mistakes.why: German capitalises nouns, not ich. The only pronoun with a capital letter mid-sentence is formal Sie.

mistakes.wrong: Wo ist die Rechnung? Es ist auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.right: Wo ist die Rechnung? Sie ist auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.why: English uses "it" for every object; German picks er, sie or es from the noun's gender. Rechnung is a die-noun, so it is sie.

mistakes.wrong: Meine Kollegen sind nett. Sie wohnt in Berlin.
mistakes.right: Meine Kollegen sind nett. Sie wohnen in Berlin.
mistakes.why: sie meaning "they" always takes the -en ending. The verb ending, not the pronoun, tells people how many.

drills.question: ___ heiße Emre.
drills.explain: The verb ending -e on heiße belongs to ich and to nobody else.

drills.question: Wie heißen ___? (you're at the Bürgeramt)
drills.explain: An official you have never met always gets the formal Sie.

drills.question: Wo wohnst ___? (your friend Ali)
drills.explain: The verb ending -st only ever pairs with du, and a friend gets du anyway.

drills.question: Wo ist der Schlüssel? ___ ist hier. (it)
drills.explain: Schlüssel is a der-noun, so the stand-in word is er even though English says "it".

drills.question: Wo ist die Rechnung? ___ ist auf dem Tisch. (it)
drills.explain: A die-noun is replaced by sie — gender decides the pronoun, not whether it's a person.
wir takes the -en ending, and the verb stays in second position.
In a question the verb comes first, and formal Sie keeps its capital letter and its -en ending.

drills.question: Meine Kollegen sind nett. ___ kommen aus Hamburg.
drills.explain: Several people means "they", which is sie — capitalised here only because it starts the sentence.

lessons.title: Present tense — regular verbs
lessons.summary: Six little endings glued onto the stem — and one present tense that covers both "I work" and "I am working".
lessons.rule:
A verb is the word that says what is happening: wohnen (to live), spielen (to play), lernen (to learn). The form you find in a dictionary is called the infinitive, and in German it nearly always ends in -en.

Cut that -en off and what is left is the stem: wohnen → wohn-, spielen → spiel-. Now you glue a small ending onto the stem, and the ending tells you who is doing it — me, you, him, us. Turkish does exactly the same thing (çalış-ıyor-um); German just has fewer and shorter endings, and there are only six to learn.

If the stem already ends in -t or -d, slide an extra -e in so the word is still sayable: arbeiten → du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet. Say arbeitst out loud once and you will understand why. Also notice that er wohnt and ihr wohnt look identical — you tell them apart from the word in front, not from the ending.

German has only one present tense. English splits I work and I am working into two different forms. German does not: Ich arbeite is both of them. There is no -ing form at all, so never build something like Ich bin arbeiten — that sentence simply does not exist in German.

The same present tense also does the job of the future. Add a time word and you are finished: Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin means I'm going to Berlin tomorrow. Germans say it this way far more often than with the longer werden-future.

tables.title: Three regular verbs side by side
When the stem ends in -t or -d: an extra -e

examples.note: Stem wohn- plus -e for ich. This is also how you say "I am living in Berlin" — same sentence, no second form.
du takes -st. English needs "are ... doing"; German gets there with one word.
er / sie / es always takes -t on the stem spiel-.
The wir form is identical to the dictionary form lernen. That is not a coincidence — both end in -en.

examples.de: Meine Frau arbeitet in einem Büro.
examples.en: My wife works in an office.
examples.note: "Meine Frau" is a she, so it behaves like er / sie / es. Stem arbeit- ends in -t, so we get -et.
Present tense doing future work. The word morgen (tomorrow) carries the time; the verb stays in the present.

mistakes.why: There is no "am ...-ing" construction in German. Copying English word for word produces a sentence Germans cannot parse — one verb with one ending is the whole thing.
The bare -en form is only for wir and sie/Sie. For er / sie / es you must swap it for -t.
The stem arbeit- already ends in -t, so an -e goes in before the ending. Same for warten, antworten, finden.
Polite Sie is not the du form dressed up — it always takes the -en ending, exactly like sie (they). You will use this every single day at work and in offices.

drills.question: Ich ___ in Berlin.
drills.explain: ich always takes -e, no matter which verb it is.

drills.question: Er ___ jeden Tag Fußball.
drills.explain: er / sie / es takes -t; the -en form would be wir or sie.

drills.question: Du ___ sehr schnell Deutsch. (lernen)
drills.explain: du is the only person that gets the -st ending.

drills.question: "I am living in Hamburg" in German is:
drills.explain: German has no continuous form, so the plain present has to cover the English -ing meaning too.

drills.question: Wir ___ um acht Uhr. (kommen)
drills.explain: wir keeps the -en, which makes it look like the dictionary form.

drills.question: Ihr ___ zu viel. (arbeiten)
drills.explain: ihr normally takes -t, but a stem ending in -t needs a linking -e first or nobody could pronounce it.
A present-tense verb plus a future time word is the normal way Germans talk about tomorrow.
"Meine Tochter" counts as she, so the verb takes the er / sie / es ending -t.

lessons.title: Stem-changing verbs — fahren, nehmen, lesen
lessons.summary: A handful of everyday verbs change their vowel — but only in the du and er/sie/es forms, nowhere else.
lessons.rule:
Some of the most common German verbs quietly change the vowel inside their stem (the part left after you remove -en). The endings stay exactly the ones you already know. Only the vowel moves.

And it happens in only two places: the du form and the er / sie / es form. ich, wir, ihr and sie / Sie are completely normal. If you remember nothing else, remember that: two forms, then back to normal.

There are three changes. a → ä: fahren (to drive/go) gives du fährst, er fährt. e → i: nehmen (to take) gives du nimmst, er nimmt. e → ie: lesen (to read) gives du liest, er liest.

Two of them need a small warning. nehmen loses its h and doubles the m — it is nimmt, not nihmt. And with lesen the stem lies- already ends in an s-sound, so the -st ending gives up its s: du liest, not du liesst. That means du and er look identical here. Same thing with essen: du isst, er isst.

There is no rule that tells you in advance which verbs do this — you learn them one at a time. The consolation is that it is a short list, and they are verbs you will say twenty times a day: fahren, nehmen, lesen, sprechen, geben, essen, schlafen, tragen, laufen, sehen.

tables.title: More of them you will meet every day

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, aber Anna fährt mit dem Rad.
examples.en: I go by bus, but Anna goes by bike.
examples.note: Same verb, same sentence: ich stays plain fahre, Anna counts as she and gets the umlaut — fährt.
nehmen → nimmst. The h disappears and the m doubles. You will hear this one in every German kitchen.

examples.de: Er liest jeden Abend die Zeitung.
examples.en: He reads the newspaper every evening.
examples.note: lesen → liest. The e stretches into ie.
sprechen → sprichst, e becomes i. Compare: ich spreche, wir sprechen — untouched.
Proof that wir keeps the plain stem. The change never leaves du and er / sie / es.
geben → gibt for er / sie / es.

mistakes.why: Once you learn nimmst / nimmt it is tempting to use that stem everywhere. The ich form never changes — it stays nehme.
The umlaut is not decoration; du fahrst is simply not a German word. a → ä in du and er / sie / es.
The opposite error: spreading the umlaut to wir. Only two persons change, and wir is not one of them.
The stem already ends in an s-sound, so the -st ending drops its s. Same with du isst (essen) and du heißt (heißen).

drills.question: Du ___ morgen nach Hamburg.
drills.explain: du triggers the a → ä change; fahrt without umlaut is the ihr form.

drills.question: Er ___ immer den Bus.
drills.explain: er / sie / es turns nehm- into nimm-, and the -t ending goes on top.

drills.question: Wir ___ am Wochenende nach Köln. (fahren)
drills.explain: wir is outside the two changing forms, so the vowel stays untouched.

drills.question: ___ du Deutsch?
drills.explain: sprechen changes e → i for du, and Spricht would be the er / sie / es form.

drills.question: Du ___ jeden Tag die Zeitung. (lesen)
drills.explain: The stem becomes lies-, and because it ends in an s-sound the ending loses its own s.

drills.question: Ihr ___ zu schnell. (sprechen)
drills.explain: ihr is a normal form — plain stem plus -t, no vowel change at all.
geben becomes gibt for er, and the verb sits in second position as usual.

drills.answer: Nimmst du den Bus oder das Auto
drills.explain: A yes/no question starts with the verb — and the du form still carries the i, so it is Nimmst, not Nehmst.

lessons.title: sein, haben, werden — the three you cannot avoid
lessons.summary: To be, to have, to become: wildly irregular, in every second sentence, and the machinery behind the past tense and the passive.
lessons.rule:
sein means to be, haben means to have, werden means to become or to get. You will use all three in your first conversation in Germany and in every one after that.

They are irregular in a way no other verbs are. Look at sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist. Not one of those looks like sein. There is nothing to work out here — these are the tables you simply memorise, and they buy you more than any other page in this course.

The tables below also give the Präteritum. That is just the grammar name for the simple past: I was, I had, it became. For most German verbs you will use a different past form in conversation, but for these three the Präteritum is what people actually say: war, hatte, wurde. "Ich war gestern krank" is normal spoken German.

These three are also helper verbs (grammar books say auxiliary) — a verb that adds no meaning of its own and just holds a bigger structure together. haben and sein build the everyday past: Ich habe gegessen (I ate), Ich bin gefahren (I went). werden builds the future and the passive — the passive is when you say what happens to something without naming who does it: Das Auto wird repariert = the car is being repaired. You do not need those yet, but every one of them runs on this page.

Finally, watch where German picks a different verb than English. Hunger, thirst and fear are things you have: Ich habe Hunger, literally "I have hunger". Your age is something you are: Ich bin 30 Jahre alt. And being cold is neither — Germans say Mir ist kalt, literally "to me it is cold". Ich bin kalt says something about your personality.

tables.title: Where German picks the other verb

examples.note: sein for jobs — and German drops the article: not "ein Ingenieur".
haben loses its b in du and er / sie / es: du hast, er hat.

examples.de: Ich habe Hunger. Gehen wir essen?
examples.en: I'm hungry. Shall we go eat?
examples.note: German owns its hunger. "Ich bin Hunger" sounds like you are claiming to be a feeling.
war is the simple past of sein and is used constantly in speech — much more than the longer past form.
werden = to become / to get. Es ist kalt would mean it already is cold.

examples.de: Wir hatten letzte Woche kein Internet.
examples.en: We had no internet last week.
examples.note: hatten — the wir form of the simple past of haben.

mistakes.why: English says "I am hungry", so the hand writes bin automatically. German treats hunger, thirst and fear as things you possess, so they take haben.
Ich bin kalt describes you as a cold person. To say your body feels cold, German puts the cold outside you: mir ist kalt, "to me it is cold".
The er / sie / es form of werden is a short irregular word, wird. You do not add -t to it, and du is wirst, not werdst.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe gestern in Köln gewesen.
mistakes.why: Two errors at once: sein never builds its past with haben, and in normal speech you would use war anyway rather than any longer form.

drills.question: Ich ___ aus der Türkei.
drills.explain: sein has a separate, unrelated word for each person — ich gets bin and nothing else.

drills.question: ___ du heute Zeit?
drills.explain: haben drops its b in the du and er forms, so the regular-looking Habst does not exist.

drills.question: Wir ___ um acht zu Hause. (sein)
drills.explain: wir and sie / Sie share the same form of sein, sind.

drills.question: Ich ___ Hunger.
drills.explain: German counts hunger as something you own rather than something you are.

drills.question: Es ___ langsam kalt. (werden)
drills.explain: werden describes a change in progress — the weather is turning cold, not simply being cold.

drills.question: Gestern ___ ich krank. (sein — Präteritum)
drills.explain: For sein the simple past is what Germans really say; the longer past form sounds heavy in conversation.
hatten is the wir form of the simple past of haben, and the verb keeps its second-position seat.
Turning an age is a change of state, so German uses werden here where English would use "is".

lessons.title: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen
lessons.summary: The six helper verbs for can, must, may, should, want and like — and why the real verb waits at the end of the sentence.
lessons.rule:
A modal verb is a helper verb. It does not say what happens — it says how you stand towards what happens: I can do it, I have to do it, I want to do it. German has six of them, and they are among the most used words in the language.

The structure never changes. The modal verb sits in slot 2 of the sentence and it is the one that takes the ending for ich / du / er. The real verb goes to the very end in its infinitive — the plain dictionary form that ends in -en (arbeiten, gehen, trinken). The infinitive never changes. Ich muss heute arbeiten. English keeps the two verbs together ("I must work today"); German pulls them apart, so you have to hold the second verb in your head until the end.

Two forms look wrong but are correct: ich and er / sie / es are identical and take no ending at all — ich kann, er kann; ich muss, sie muss; ich darf, es darf. Adding a -t or an -e here is the classic beginner slip.

The difference that matters in real life: Ich muss nicht arbeiten means I don't have to work — nobody is forcing me, wonderful. Ich darf nicht arbeiten means I am not allowed to work — it is forbidden, a problem. English "I must not" means the second one, so translating word for word flips your meaning into the opposite. When you want to say something is banned, reach for dürfen + nicht.

Finally, möchten ("would like") is the polite branch of mögen and the normal way to ask for anything in a shop, a bakery or an office: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie möchten. Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Ich will einen Kaffee is correct German but lands like a demand.

tables.title: müssen + nicht is NOT dürfen + nicht
rows: The obligation is gone. You are free.
I am not allowed to work.

examples.note: kann carries the ending, kommen stays in its dictionary form at the very end.

examples.de: Wir müssen um acht Uhr am Bahnhof sein.
examples.en: We have to be at the station at eight.
examples.note: Even sein goes to the end as an infinitive. Everything else squeezes in before it.

examples.en: You're not allowed to park here.
examples.note: darf nicht = forbidden. This is the sentence on half the signs in Germany.
musst nicht cancels the duty — it is not a ban. You may wait if you like.
möchten is the standard polite request at any counter or office.

examples.de: Am Wochenende will er lange schlafen.
examples.en: At the weekend he wants to sleep in.
examples.note: The sentence starts with a time, so the modal stays in slot 2 and er moves behind it.

mistakes.why: English keeps the two verbs together, German does not. The second verb is always the last word — objects, times and places all come before it.

mistakes.wrong: Ich muss nicht rauchen. (meaning: smoking is forbidden)
mistakes.why: müssen + nicht only removes an obligation. To say something is not allowed you need dürfen + nicht, otherwise you have said the opposite of what you meant.
Modal verbs take no ending for ich and er/sie/es — those two forms are identical and bare.

mistakes.wrong: Ich will ein Bier. (to a waiter)
mistakes.why: wollen is a blunt 'I want'. In shops, restaurants and offices Germans use möchten — it is the normal register, not extra formality.

drills.question: Ich ___ heute nicht arbeiten. (können)
drills.explain: The ich form of a modal verb takes no ending at all — that is what makes this group special.

drills.question: Er ___ um sechs Uhr aufstehen. (müssen)
drills.explain: For er/sie/es a modal looks exactly like the ich form, so there is no -t on the end.

drills.question: Wir ___ hier nicht parken. (dürfen)
drills.explain: For wir the modal goes back to the plain infinitive form, so it looks like the dictionary entry.
The modal takes slot 2 and the second verb is pushed all the way to the end, behind the object.

drills.question: There is a no-smoking sign. Which sentence tells someone smoking is FORBIDDEN?
drills.explain: Only dürfen + nicht expresses a ban; müssen + nicht just means there is no obligation.

drills.question: Es ist Samstag. Ich ___ nicht arbeiten. (= I don't have to)
drills.explain: 'Not having to' is the absence of duty, which is exactly what müssen + nicht expresses.
In a yes/no question the modal jumps to the front, but the second verb still waits at the end.

drills.answer: Am Wochenende will er lange schlafen
drills.explain: Starting with a time expression pushes the subject behind the modal, because the modal must stay in slot 2.

lessons.title: Nominativ — the subject
lessons.summary: German labels a noun's job in the sentence. Nominativ is the label for the doer — and it is the form you already learned.
lessons.rule:
Every noun in a sentence has a job: it is doing something, or something is being done to it, or something is being given to it. German labels that job, and the label system is called case. Turkish does this with endings glued onto the noun (ev, evi, eve). German does it differently: it leaves the noun alone and changes the little word in front of it — der, die, das, ein, mein.

There are four cases. This is the first and by far the easiest: Nominativ. It marks the subject — the person or thing that is doing the verb. To find it, ask one question: who or what is doing this? In Der Zug kommt um acht. — who or what is coming? The train. So der Zug is nominative.

The best news in this whole topic: the nominative is the dictionary form. When you learn der Tisch, die Lampe, das Fenster, you have already learned the nominative. There is nothing extra to change.

German also insists that the subject is actually said. Turkish can drop it (geliyorum); German cannot — Ich komme. keeps the ich, always. And when nothing is really doing anything, German still puts a placeholder in the slot: Es regnet. Es ist kalt.

One thing surprises everybody: after sein (to be), werden (to become) and bleiben (to stay), the word after the verb is also nominative. These three verbs don't do anything to anything — they put an equals sign between two things. So it is Das ist ein Hund., never einen Hund. Same with Er wird Vater. and Das bleibt ein Problem.

tables.title: Nominativ — the word in front of the noun
Nominative on BOTH sides of the verb

examples.note: Who or what is hot? The coffee. It is the subject, so it keeps its dictionary form der.
The flat is doing the costing — feminine subject, so die.
After ist nothing changes. Both das and ein Hund are nominative.
mein has no ending here because Kollege is masculine and it is the subject.
Nothing is really doing the raining, but German still needs a word in the subject slot: es.
wer is the nominative question word — it asks specifically for the doer.

mistakes.why: Turkish can leave the subject out, German never can. Something must fill the subject slot, even if it is only das or es.
Gender is fixed per noun and has nothing to do with meaning. Always learn the noun together with its article: der Mann, die Frau, das Kind.
sein never creates an object. Nothing is happening to the dog, so it stays nominative — ein, not einen.
With jobs after sein or werden, German drops the article completely. The same goes for nationality: Ich bin Türke.

drills.question: ___ Mann arbeitet in Berlin.
drills.explain: The man is the one doing the working, and the doer always gets the plain nominative form.

drills.question: Das ist ___ Auto.
drills.explain: sein just links two things, so the word after it stays in the dictionary form.

drills.question: ___ Handy ist neu. (neuter noun)
drills.explain: The phone is the thing doing the 'being new', so the neuter subject form das is what you need.
The doer comes first and the verb takes slot 2 — the normal shape of a German statement.

drills.question: Wer ist der Chef? — ___ ist der Chef.
drills.explain: The pronoun here is the one doing the verb, and only er is the subject form.

drills.question: ___ Kinder spielen draußen.
drills.explain: Every plural noun uses die as its subject word, no matter what gender the single noun has.
After ist the second part is still nominative, which is why mein carries no ending.

drills.question: Der Kaffee kostet zwei Euro. Which part is the subject — the one doing the verb?
drills.explain: Ask 'who or what is doing the costing?' — the coffee is, and that answer is always the nominative.

lessons.title: Akkusativ — the direct object
lessons.summary: Who or what is receiving the action — and the great relief that only masculine visibly changes.
lessons.rule:
Most verbs do something to something. Ich trinke den Kaffee. — the drinking lands on the coffee. The thing on the receiving end is called the direct object, and German marks it with the Akkusativ case.

There is a simple test. Say the subject and the verb, then ask wen oder was? ('whom or what?'). Ich kaufe … wen oder was? → einen Apfel. Whatever answers that question is the accusative.

Now the relief. Of the four genders, only masculine actually changes: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen, mein → meinen. Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly the same as in the nominative. Three quarters of the job is doing nothing at all — so when you spot a masculine noun as the object, that -n is the only thing you have to remember.

The pronouns do change, and you will use these hourly:
ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, sie → sie, es → es, wir → uns, ihr → euch, sie/Sie → sie/Sie.

Some words switch the accusative on automatically, no thinking required. After durch, für, gegen, ohne, um the following noun is always accusative, even when nothing is receiving any action at all. And two everyday verbs always take an accusative object: haben and es gibt — Ich habe einen Termin. Es gibt hier einen Supermarkt.

tables.title: The definite article: nominative vs accusative
ein, kein, mein — same single change
Prepositions that always trigger the accusative
rows: Ich habe nichts gegen den Plan.
Ich gehe nie ohne meinen Ausweis.

examples.note: I take wen oder was? The salad. Der Salat is masculine, so it becomes den Salat.
der Kaffee is masculine, so ein becomes einen. Probably the most useful accusative in Germany.
Neuter, so absolutely nothing changes — das stays das.
The park isn't receiving any action, but durch forces the accusative anyway.
für always takes the accusative, and pronouns feel it too: du becomes dich.
haben always takes an accusative object, so der Termin becomes einen Termin.

mistakes.why: The man is what the seeing lands on, and masculine is the one gender that visibly changes: der → den.
haben always takes an accusative object, and Termin is masculine, so ein must become einen.
für switches on the accusative automatically, and pronouns change form there: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn.
Kaffee is masculine (der Kaffee), not feminine. The accusative ending is only right if you learned the gender right.

drills.question: Die Frau sucht den Schlüssel. Which part is the direct object — the thing the action lands on?
drills.explain: Ask 'sie sucht wen oder was?' — whatever answers that question is the accusative object.

drills.question: Ich trinke ___ Kaffee.
drills.explain: The coffee is what the drinking lands on, and masculine der becomes den in the accusative.

drills.question: Ich lese ___ Buch. (das Buch)
drills.explain: Neuter nouns look identical in the nominative and the accusative, so there is nothing to change.
Subject first, verb in slot 2, then the object — and masculine ein turns into einen.

drills.question: Wir gehen durch ___ Park.
drills.explain: durch is one of the five prepositions that force the accusative, no matter what the sentence means.

drills.question: Das Geschenk ist für ___. (ich)
drills.explain: Pronouns take accusative forms too, and für always demands the accusative.

drills.answer: Ich gehe nie ohne meinen Ausweis
drills.explain: ohne is an automatic accusative trigger, so mein has to become meinen before a masculine noun.

drills.question: Den Kuchen isst der Mann. Who is doing the eating?
drills.explain: German shows the job through the article rather than the position, so der Mann is the doer even standing at the end.

lessons.title: Dativ — the indirect object
lessons.summary: The person on the receiving end — and the everyday verbs that force it when English gives you no warning at all.
lessons.rule:
A lot of German sentences have two things after the verb. Take I give my friend the book. There are two nouns there: the book (the thing that moves) and my friend (the person who ends up holding it).

The thing the action lands on directly — the book — is the direct object, and German marks it with the Akkusativ. The person who receives — my friend — is the indirect object, and German marks it with the Dativ. The English test: could you put to or for in front of it? I give the book to my friend. Yes → Dativ.

The German test question is Wem?, meaning to whom? Ask Ich gebe wem das Buch? The answer is dem Freund — and that answer is your Dativ.

The articles change like this: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, and plural die → den. In the plural the noun itself also gets an extra -n: die Kinder → den Kindern, die Freunde → den Freunden. If the plural already ends in -n or -s, leave it alone: den Frauen, den Autos.

The endings are the easy part. The hard part is that some very common German verbs demand the Dativ where English gives you no clue whatsoever. It is Ich helfe dir, never Ich helfe dich. Learn these seven as one block: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, passen, schmecken, antworten.

tables.title: Dativ forms of ein, kein, mein
Personal pronouns in all three cases

examples.note: mir, not mich. Probably the single most useful Dativ sentence you will say in Germany.
helfen always takes the Dativ, so mein Bruder becomes meinem Bruder — even though English 'my brother' looks like a plain object.

examples.en: The car belongs to my sister.
examples.note: gehören = Dativ. Feminine die → der, so meine → meiner.

examples.en: I like the flat a lot.
examples.note: Literally 'the flat pleases me'. The flat is the subject; the person doing the liking sits in the Dativ.

examples.de: Ich kaufe den Kindern ein Eis.
examples.en: I'm buying the children an ice cream.
examples.note: Plural Dativ: die Kinder → den Kindern. The article changes and the noun picks up an -n.
schmecken = Dativ. uns is luckily the same in Akkusativ and Dativ, so nothing to get wrong here.

mistakes.why: helfen is a Dativ verb. English 'help me' feels like a direct object, but German treats it as giving help TO someone.
danken is also a Dativ verb — thanks go TO a person. Note that für afterwards is still Akkusativ, so the two cases sit side by side.
Feminine Dativ is der — the exact same word as the masculine Nominativ. It looks wrong, but der Frau here means 'to the woman'.
In the Dativ plural the noun itself takes an extra -n, not just the article.

drills.question: Ich helfe ___ Mann.
drills.explain: helfen forces the Dativ no matter what the sentence looks like, and masculine Dativ is dem.

drills.question: Das Handy gehört ___ Frau.
drills.explain: gehören takes the Dativ, and feminine Dativ is der — the form that looks like a masculine article.

drills.question: Kannst du ___ helfen? (ich)
drills.explain: The Dativ form of ich is mir, and helfen never accepts mich.

drills.question: Die Suppe schmeckt ___ gut.
drills.explain: With schmecken the food is the subject and the person tasting it is the receiver, so Dativ.

drills.question: Ich spiele mit den ___. (die Kinder)
drills.explain: mit is a Dativ preposition, and Dativ plural nouns add -n.

drills.question: ___ gehört das Fahrrad?
drills.explain: You are asking to whom the bike belongs, and the question word for the Dativ is wem.

drills.answer: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel
drills.explain: When both objects are nouns, the receiver in the Dativ comes before the thing in the Akkusativ.
With gefallen the liked thing is the subject, so the person doing the liking is pushed into the Dativ: mein → meinem.

lessons.title: Genitiv — possession
lessons.summary: The case that says whose — the one you need to read on signs and contracts, but can almost always avoid speaking.
lessons.rule:
The Genitiv is the case that answers whose? English does this two ways: the man's car or the roof of the house. Turkish does it with -in / -ın. German does it by changing the article — and it puts the owner after the thing owned.

So the man's car is das Auto des Mannes — literally the car of-the man. Owner second. Always.

The articles: masculine der → des, feminine die → der, neuter das → des, plural die → der. On top of that, masculine and neuter nouns take an extra -s or -es: des Autos, des Kindes, des Mannes. Short one-syllable words usually take -es, longer ones just -s. Feminine and plural nouns never change at all.

Now the good news. Spoken German is quietly dropping the Genitiv. Almost nobody in a café says das Auto meines Bruders — they say das Auto von meinem Bruder, using von + Dativ. So learn to recognise the Genitiv in rental contracts, signs and newspapers, but feel free to go months without ever producing one.

The place you cannot dodge it is after three very common little words: wegen (because of), während (during) and trotz (despite). Correct German wants the Genitiv after them — wegen des Wetters. In real speech you will constantly hear the Dativ instead — wegen dem Wetter — and nobody blinks.

tables.title: The definite article — all four cases

examples.de: Das ist das Auto meines Bruders.
examples.note: The owner comes second. Masculine, so mein → meines and Bruder picks up an -s.

examples.de: Das ist das Auto von meinem Bruder.
examples.note: Same meaning, and this is what you will actually hear. von + Dativ, so mein → meinem.

examples.de: Die Farbe der Tür gefällt mir nicht.
examples.en: I don't like the colour of the door.
examples.note: Tür is feminine, so die → der. The noun itself stays completely unchanged.

examples.de: Wegen des Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.en: Because of the weather we're staying home.
examples.note: wegen wants the Genitiv: das Wetter → des Wetters.

examples.de: Während der Woche arbeite ich viel.
examples.en: During the week I work a lot.
examples.note: während + Genitiv. die Woche is feminine, so die → der and Woche is untouched.

examples.de: Trotz des Regens gehen wir spazieren.
examples.en: Despite the rain we're going for a walk.
examples.note: trotz + Genitiv. der Regen is masculine → des Regens.

mistakes.right: Das ist das Auto meines Bruders.
mistakes.why: German does not copy the English owner-in-front order for normal nouns. Only bare first names go in front: Emres Auto.

mistakes.wrong: Das ist das Auto von mein Bruder.
mistakes.right: Das ist das Auto von meinem Bruder.
mistakes.why: von always takes the Dativ, so mein becomes meinem. Escaping the Genitiv does not mean escaping cases.
Tür is feminine (die Tür), and feminine Genitiv is der. des only ever belongs to masculine and neuter.
German has no apostrophe before the possessive -s. Write it straight onto the name.

drills.question: Das ist das Auto ___ Mannes.
drills.explain: Masculine Genitiv is des, and the -es already sitting on Mannes confirms it.

drills.question: Die Farbe ___ Tür ist schön.
drills.explain: Tür is feminine, and feminine Genitiv is der — des only works for masculine and neuter.

drills.question: Wegen ___ Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause. (das Wetter)
drills.explain: wegen forces the Genitiv, and neuter das becomes des.

drills.question: Das ist das Zimmer des ___. (das Kind)
drills.explain: Masculine and neuter nouns add -s or -es in the Genitiv, and short words like Kind prefer -es.

drills.question: Which is the normal spoken version of "das Haus meiner Eltern"?
drills.explain: von always takes the Dativ, and the Dativ plural of meine is meinen.

drills.question: Trotz ___ Regens gehen wir spazieren.
drills.explain: trotz takes the Genitiv and der Regen is masculine, so the article becomes des.

drills.answer: Das ist die Tasche meiner Schwester
drills.explain: The owner always follows the thing owned, and feminine Genitiv turns meine into meiner.

drills.answer: Während der Woche arbeite ich viel
drills.explain: während takes the Genitiv (der Woche), and because that phrase opens the sentence the verb arbeite has to stay in position two.

lessons.title: All four cases side by side
lessons.summary: The complete article table plus a four-step procedure for picking the right case in any sentence.
lessons.rule:
This is your reference page. Four cases, three genders, plus plural — and it really comes down to three tables you will end up knowing by heart.

What the four cases are for, in plain words:

  • Nominativ — the doer. Who or what is performing the verb. Der Mann schläft.
  • Akkusativ — the thing the verb lands on directly. Ich sehe den Mann.
  • Dativ — the receiver: to whom, for whom. Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
  • Genitiv — the owner: whose. das Auto des Mannes

How to decide, every single time. Work through it in this order and stop as soon as you get an answer:

  • 1. Is there a preposition in front of the noun? If yes, it decides and nothing else matters. mit is always Dativ, für is always Akkusativ. (A handful — in, auf, an, unter, über — go both ways: Dativ for where something is, Akkusativ for where it is going.)
  • 2. Find the verb. Then ask wer? — who is doing it? That noun is the Nominativ.
  • 3. Ask wem? — who receives it, who is it for? That noun is the Dativ. Watch out for the Dativ verbs: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, passen, schmecken, antworten.
  • 4. Ask wen? or was? — what is directly affected? That noun is the Akkusativ.

Two shortcuts worth memorising instead of the whole grid: in the masculine column everything changes (der / den / dem / des), and feminine and neuter never change between Nominativ and Akkusativ. Most of the time your only real decision is what to do with a masculine noun.

lessons.title: mein, dein, sein, ihr — possessive articles
lessons.summary: One set of endings covers my, your, his, her, our and their — the exact same endings ein and kein already use.
lessons.rule:
A possessive is the little word that says who something belongs to: my bag, your car, her brother. Turkish glues this onto the noun as a suffix — çanta-m — but German puts a separate word in front of the noun, in the very same slot where der or ein would go. So you say meine Tasche, never die meine Tasche. One slot, one word.

Here is the good news, and it really is the whole lesson: possessives take exactly the same endings as ein and kein. If you can already say einen Bruder, then you can say meinen Bruder, deinen Bruder, seinen Bruder, unseren Bruder. Eight words, one pattern.

Think of every possessive as two pieces stuck together. The front piece says whose it is and follows the owner: mein-, dein-, sein-, ihr-. The ending ignores the owner completely — it reacts only to the noun that comes next: is that noun a der, die or das word, and what job is it doing in the sentence? German calls those jobs cases:

  • Nominative — the doer of the sentence: Mein Bruder kommt.
  • Accusative — the thing the action lands on: Ich suche meinen Bruder.
  • Dative — the receiver, and whatever follows mit, bei, zu: Ich fahre mit meinem Bruder.

So in Anna sucht ihren Bruder, ihr- is there because Anna is female, and -en is there because der Bruder is masculine and is the thing being searched for. The two halves have nothing to do with each other.

Two of these words are famously confusing. sein means his — and also its. ihr means her — and also their. And Ihr with a capital I in the middle of a sentence means your, when you address someone politely as Sie. Only that capital letter separates the last two, so write it carefully in emails and forms. One spelling wrinkle too: euer (your, to several friends) drops its second e as soon as an ending appears — euer Auto but eure Wohnung, euren Bruder. Nobody says eueren.

lessons.title: The verb goes second — always
lessons.summary: In a German statement the conjugated verb is the second element, no matter what you put first — and the subject moves behind it.
lessons.rule:
If you learn one structural rule in German, learn this one: in a normal statement the conjugated verb sits in position 2. "Conjugated" just means the form that has changed to match the person doing it — ich gehe, du gehst, wir gehen. Position 2 means: exactly one thing stands before it, then the verb.

And position 2 counts chunks of meaning, not words. Everything in front of the verb has to be one single unit — one idea. Ich is a chunk. Morgen is a chunk. Morgen früh um sechs Uhr is still one chunk, because it is one piece of information about time. Whatever you choose, only that one chunk is allowed in front of the verb.

Now the consequence that feels strange at first. If you put something other than the subject in front — a time word, a place, a linking word — the subject does not disappear. It jumps behind the verb. Ich gehe heute ins Kino. becomes Heute gehe ich ins Kino. Never Heute ich gehe... That is the loudest foreign-accent mistake in German, and it is exactly what English and Turkish word order push you towards.

Germans front things constantly, because position 1 is where you put whatever the sentence is really about, or whatever links it to the sentence before: Dann fahre ich nach Hause. Deshalb lerne ich Deutsch. In Berlin ist das normal. The verb itself never moves — everything else rearranges around it.

Two footnotes. The glue words und, aber, oder, denn sit outside the sentence, so they do not fill position 1: Aber ich habe keine Zeit. is correct. And this rule describes main clauses — a piece that could stand alone as a complete sentence. Words like weil and dass build a different kind of clause that kicks the verb all the way to the end, which is its own lesson.

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.summary: Two shapes only: verb first for yes/no questions, question word first for everything else — plus the wo / wohin / woher split.
lessons.rule:
German asks questions in exactly two shapes, and neither one needs a helper word. English sticks do in front — Do you live here? German has nothing like that. You simply move the verb.

Shape 1 — yes/no questions. Take the statement and put the conjugated verb right at the front. "Conjugated" means the form that changed to match the person: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt. So Du wohnst hier. becomes Wohnst du hier? The subject follows immediately after it.

Shape 2 — W-questions. Start with the question word (nearly all of them begin with w), then the verb, then the subject: Wo wohnst du? Wann kommt der Zug? This is not a new rule at all — the W-word is simply filling position 1, and the verb is still the second element, exactly as in a statement.

The part that trips up every English speaker is wo / wohin / woher. English uses where for all three. German splits them, and here Turkish helps you far more than English does: wo = nerede, wohin = nereye, woher = nereden. If the verb involves movement (gehen, fahren, kommen), you almost certainly need wohin or woher, not wo.

Answering: ja for yes, nein for no — and doch, which English has no word for. Use doch to contradict a negative question: Kommst du nicht mit? — Doch! meaning "Yes, I actually am coming."

lessons.title: Separable verbs — the prefix flies to the end
lessons.summary: Half the verb breaks off and waits at the very end of the sentence — so you cannot know what a German verb means until you hear the last word.
lessons.rule:
A prefix is a small piece stuck onto the front of a verb that changes what it means. stehen means to stand. Put auf in front and aufstehen means to get up. Same core verb, completely different action. rufen is to shout; anrufen is to phone someone.

Now the German twist. In a normal statement — a main clause, meaning a chunk that could stand alone as a complete sentence — that prefix does not stay attached. The verb splits in two. The conjugated half (the half that changed to match the person: ich stehe, du stehst) stays in position 2 where verbs always are, and the prefix flies all the way to the end of the sentence:
aufstehen → Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
anrufen → Ich rufe dich heute Abend an.
einkaufen → Wir kaufen am Samstag ein.

This has a real consequence for listening: you cannot understand a German sentence until you have heard the last word. Ich rufe meine Mutter… is not finished — with an at the end it means I am phoning her, without it, I am shouting for her. Turkish speakers have an advantage here, because you are already used to waiting until the end of a sentence for the verb. Do exactly that in German: the final word is very often the half that carries the meaning.

Which prefixes split? A reliable rule of thumb: if the prefix is also a word you already know on its own, it splits. If it is a meaningless syllable, it never moves. Your ear can decide it too — separable prefixes are stressed: AUFstehen, ANrufen. Inseparable ones are not: beSUchen, verKAUfen.

  • Separable (these fly to the end): auf- an- aus- ein- mit- ab- zu- vor- nach- zurück- weg-
  • Inseparable (these never move): be- ge- er- ver- ent- emp- miss- zer-

Two situations keep the verb in one piece. After a modal verb like müssen or können, the second verb goes to the end whole and unchanged: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen. And the dictionary form is always written joined. In the past tense the two halves grip a ge between them: aufgestanden, angerufen, eingekauft.

lessons.title: Perfekt — how Germans talk about the past
lessons.summary: Two pieces: haben or sein in position 2, and the frozen participle form at the very end of the sentence.
lessons.rule:
When a German tells you what they did yesterday, they use the Perfekt. This is the everyday past tense of spoken German — for holidays, for work, for what you had for lunch. Turkish does this with one word and a suffix (gittim). German needs two pieces, and they end up at opposite ends of the sentence.

Piece one is a helper verb — a verb that carries no meaning of its own and is only there to hold the grammar. German has exactly two: haben or sein. It is conjugated normally and sits in position 2, where the verb always is. Piece two is the past participle: one fixed form of the real verb that never changes for person, and it is parked at the very end of the sentence. Everything you want to say gets sandwiched in between:
Ich habe gestern Abend einen Film gesehen.

Building the participle. Regular verbs take ge + the stem + t: machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, spielen → gespielt. Irregular verbs take ge + the stem + en, usually with a vowel change inside: gehen → gegangen, sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken. There are around a hundred common irregular ones and they have to be learned one by one, like English go / gone.

Two groups take no ge at all: verbs ending in -ieren (studieren → studiert, telefonieren → telefoniert) and verbs with an inseparable prefix (besuchen → besucht, verkaufen → verkauft). Separable verbs are the opposite — the ge slots into the middle: aufstehen → aufgestanden, einkaufen → eingekauft.

Now the choice that worries everybody: haben or sein. About nine verbs in ten take haben, so make that your default. Use sein when the verb is movement from A to B (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen) or a change of state, where you are one thing before and something else after (aufstehen, einschlafen, werden, sterben) — plus the two odd ones you simply memorise, sein and bleiben. English gives you no help here at all, since English uses have for everything.

lessons.title: Präteritum — the written past
lessons.summary: A one-word past you mostly need to recognise in writing — except for war, hatte and the modals, which you will say every single day.
lessons.rule:
German has a second past tense: the Präteritum. It is one word instead of two — ich ging where the Perfekt says ich bin gegangen. Both mean exactly the same thing, I went. The difference is not meaning. It is where you are allowed to use them.

Präteritum lives in writing: novels, newspapers, reports, the news on television, fairy tales. Perfekt lives in speech. If you say Ich ging gestern ins Kino to a colleague at lunch, you sound like a man reading aloud from a book. Say Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen. So for most verbs, this lesson is a recognise it lesson — you need to understand er sah, sie kam, er sagte on a page, and never produce them yourself.

But there is a small group that goes the other way. These use the Präteritum even in conversation, and using the Perfekt for them sounds clumsy and foreign. This group you must produce, actively, from day one:

  • sein → war: Ich war gestern nicht im Büro.
  • haben → hatte: Ich hatte keine Zeit.
  • the modals: können → konnte, müssen → musste, wollen → wollte, dürfen → durfte, sollen → sollte
  • es gibt → es gab: Es gab ein Problem.

How the forms are built, for reading. Regular verbs push -te- in before the ending: machen → ich machte, du machtest, er machte. Irregular verbs change the vowel and add nothing: gehen → ging, kommen → kam, sehen → sah, fahren → fuhr. The one thing that always gives it away: in the Präteritum, ich and er/sie/es are identical — ich war / er war, ich ging / er ging. There is no -t on the third person the way there is in the present.

One trap worth marking now. konnte and könnte are two different words, and so are musste and müsste. The plain vowel is the past: I could / I had to. The two dots make it a polite or hypothetical form: I would be able to / I would have to. In the past there is never an umlaut.

lessons.title: Prepositions that always take Akkusativ
lessons.summary: Seven little words that push the next noun into the Akkusativ automatically — the meaning is irrelevant, you just learn the list.
lessons.rule:
A preposition is one of those small words that sits in front of a noun and states the relation: for you, without sugar, through the city. Turkish does this job with an ending glued onto the word (şekersiz) or with a word that follows it (senin için). German puts it in front, like English — but charges you one extra fee.

In German every preposition owns a case. A case is just the small change German makes to the article in front of a noun depending on the noun's job: der Mann can become den Mann or dem Mann. Normally you have to work the case out from the meaning. After a preposition you work out nothing — the preposition has already decided, and you obey.

Seven prepositions always demand the Akkusativ. Not usually. Not when something moves. Always. Learn them as one block: FUDGEBO — für, um, durch, gegen, entlang, bis, ohne.

Luckily the Akkusativ is the cheap case, because only the masculine visibly changes: der → den, ein → einen, mein → meinen. Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly like the dictionary form. Pronouns do change, though, and this is where people get caught: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns. You say für dich, never für du.

Two footnotes. entlang is the odd one out: it stands after its noun — die Straße entlang, not entlang die Straße. And bis usually appears bare in front of a time or a place — bis morgen, bis Berlin. If a second preposition follows, that second one takes over: bis zum Bahnhof is Dativ, because zu is in charge now.

der Bruder is masculine, and masculine after an Akkusativ preposition adds -en: mein → meinen.

entlang is the one preposition on this list that stands behind its noun, exactly like a Turkish postposition.

drills.question: Das Geschenk ist für ___.
drills.explain: für is on the Akkusativ list, and the Akkusativ form of du is dich.

drills.question: Wir gehen durch ___ Park.
drills.explain: durch always takes the Akkusativ, and masculine is the only form that visibly changes: der → den.

drills.question: Ich fahre ohne ___ Auto. (mein)

drills.question: Der Bäcker ist um ___ Ecke.
drills.explain: Nothing is moving, but um demands the Akkusativ anyway; feminine simply looks the same as the Nominativ.

drills.question: Ich habe nichts gegen ___. (er)
drills.explain: gegen takes the Akkusativ, and er is the pronoun that changes most obviously: er → ihn.

drills.explain: der Vater is masculine and für is an Akkusativ preposition, so mein takes the -en ending.

lessons.title: Prepositions that always take Dativ
lessons.summary: The chant every German schoolchild knows — aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu — plus the contractions you cannot avoid and the nach/zu/in trap.
lessons.rule:
Same deal as the last lesson, different case. These prepositions do not think either: whatever noun follows them goes into the Dativ, every single time, whatever the sentence means.

The core list is chanted in German schools as seven words in a row: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Say it out loud until it sounds like one long word. Then add three quieter ones you will still meet weekly: gegenüber (opposite), ab (from … onwards), außer (except).

The Dativ changes more than the Akkusativ did, so there is more to see: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, and plural die → den with an extra -n on the noun itself, as in mit den Kindern. Pronouns: ich → mir, du → dir, er → ihm, sie → ihr, wir → uns.

Four of these fuse with the article in everyday speech, and the fused form is not optional — the long version sounds like you are pointing at one specific thing:

  • zu dem → zum — zum Arzt
  • zu der → zur — zur Arbeit
  • von dem → vom — vom Bahnhof
  • bei dem → beim — beim Chef

Now the part that trips up everybody living in Germany: how to say to a place. German splits it three ways. Use nach for towns and countries that have no article — nach Berlin, nach Deutschland — plus the fixed phrase nach Hause. Use zu for people, shops and institutions you are heading for — zum Arzt, zur Arbeit, zu Anna. Use in when you actually go inside something, and for countries that carry an article — in die Stadt, in den Supermarkt, in die Türkei. Watch out: that last in is not on this list and takes the Akkusativ instead. The next lesson is entirely about it.

lessons.title: The two-way prepositions — in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen
lessons.summary: Nine prepositions that take either case, and the single question — wohin? or wo? — that decides which one.
lessons.rule:
Nine prepositions refuse to pick a side. They take the Akkusativ sometimes and the Dativ other times, and the very same words mean two different things depending on which one you choose. They are: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.

There is exactly one test and it takes two seconds. Ask the sentence a question:

  • wohin? — where to? Something ends up in a new place. → Akkusativ: Ich gehe in die Küche.
  • wo? — where? You are only reporting a position. → Dativ: Ich bin in der Küche.

Read the next bit slowly, because it is the trap that catches everyone: the test is not "is anything moving". It is "does something cross into a new place". Ich schwimme im See is full of movement, but all of it happens inside the lake and I never enter the lake during the sentence — Dativ. Ich springe in den See — now I cross the edge and end up somewhere I was not before — Akkusativ.

The verb usually gives the answer away. sein, bleiben, wohnen, arbeiten, stehen, liegen, sitzen, warten describe a position → Dativ. gehen, fahren, kommen, stellen, legen, setzen, hängen put something somewhere new → Akkusativ. German even keeps two versions of the same idea: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch (it is lying there) against Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch (I am putting it there).

Several of these fuse with the article, and the short form hands you the case for free: ins and ans are Akkusativ, im and am are Dativ. So Ich gehe ins Kino means you are on your way to the cinema, and Ich bin im Kino means you are already sitting inside it. One letter, a completely different sentence.

lessons.title: weil, dass, wenn — the verb goes to the END
lessons.summary: Eight little words — weil, dass, wenn, ob and friends — that kick the conjugated verb all the way to the back of its own clause.
lessons.rule:
A clause is a piece of a sentence that has its own subject and its own verb. Ich bleibe zu Hause is a clause. So is weil ich krank bin — but notice the difference. The first one can stand alone as a whole sentence. The second one cannot: say weil ich krank bin to someone out of the blue and they will stand there waiting for the rest. That second kind is a subordinate clause — a piece that hangs off a main sentence and explains it, qualifies it or reports it.

German marks these clauses with a signal word at the front: weil (because), dass (that), wenn (if / whenever), ob (whether), obwohl (although), damit (so that), bevor (before), als (when, one time in the past). The moment one of those appears, one thing happens, and it always happens: the conjugated verb slides to the very end of that clause. "Conjugated" just means the form that changed to match the person doing it — ich bin, er kommt, wir haben. And there is always a comma in front of the signal word.

So Ich bin krank turns into …, weil ich krank bin. Nothing else moves; only the verb travels. This should feel less alien to you than it does to an English speaker, because Turkish puts the verb at the end too. The hard part is not the idea — it is doing it at speaking speed, since weil comes out of your mouth long before you have decided which verb will finish the sentence.

Three situations where people lose the thread. With a modal verb (muss, kann, will), the modal is the conjugated one, so it goes last and the plain verb waits just in front of it: …, weil ich arbeiten muss. With a separable verb — one whose little prefix normally flies off to the end, like ich rufe dich an — the two halves glue back together into a single word: …, dass ich dich anrufe. And in the past, habe or bin is the conjugated part, so that is what lands last: …, weil ich zu viel gegessen habe.

Two warnings. First, if you put the subordinate clause first, the whole clause counts as one single chunk in position 1, so the main verb must come immediately after the comma: Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause. You end up with two verbs meeting around the comma — bin, bleibe — which looks broken to a beginner and is exactly right. Second, do not over-apply this. denn means the same as weil, and und, aber and oder join things too, but all four are plain joiners that change nothing: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.

drills.explain: The verb still has to match ich, but weil parks it in the last slot, after krank.

drills.explain: The modal muss is the conjugated verb, so it takes the final slot and the plain arbeiten stands in front of it.

drills.explain: The main clause keeps its normal shape; only inside the weil-clause does fährt jump to the end.

drills.explain: In a subordinate clause the prefix an- glues back onto ruft and the whole word goes last.

drills.explain: The whole wenn-clause counts as one chunk in position 1, so the main verb has to come straight after the comma.

lessons.title: Joining sentences: und, aber, denn, oder, sondern, deshalb
lessons.summary: Three kinds of glue between sentences: some change nothing, some flip the subject behind the verb, some throw the verb to the end.
lessons.rule:
Once you can build one sentence, you want to stick two of them together. German has three different kinds of glue for that, and they all look equally harmless — but each one does something different to the word order. Choosing the right glue and then getting the order right is most of what makes a beginner suddenly sound fluent.

Group 1: the plain joiners. und (and), aber (but), oder (or), denn (because), sondern (but rather). These five stand outside both sentences, in a kind of position zero. They change nothing. Whatever the second half would have looked like on its own, that is what you say: Ich bin müde, aber ich komme mit. Subject first, verb second, exactly as normal.

Group 2: the connectors. deshalb (that's why), trotzdem (even so), dann (then), außerdem (besides), danach (after that). These are real words inside the sentence, and they are greedy — they take position 1 for themselves. Since the conjugated verb has to be in position 2, the subject gets pushed behind it: Es regnet. Deshalb nehme ich den Bus. Never Deshalb ich nehme. If you remember one thing from this lesson, remember that this group flips subject and verb.

Group 3: the subordinators. weil, dass, wenn, obwohl and their friends. These send the conjugated verb all the way to the end of their own clause: Ich nehme den Bus, weil es regnet. Notice that one single thought can be said with all three kinds of glue, and only the word order tells them apart: …, denn es regnet / …, weil es regnet / Deshalb nehme ich den Bus.

Finally, the pair that trips up everybody: aber versus sondern. Both come out as "but" in English and as ama in Turkish, so nothing in your head warns you. Use sondern only when the first half was negative — it had nicht or kein in it — and the second half replaces the thing you just cancelled: Das ist kein Tee, sondern Kaffee. Ich komme nicht heute, sondern morgen. If the second half adds something new instead of replacing it, you stay with aber, negative or not: Ich habe kein Auto, aber ich habe ein Fahrrad.
