lessons.title: Adjective endings — the scary table, made manageable
lessons.summary: No ending after ist, always an ending before a noun — and one simple idea that makes the three-part table finally make sense.
lessons.rule:
An adjective is a describing word: neu (new), alt (old), groß (big), klein (small), kalt (cold). In German an adjective can stand in two very different places, and the whole lesson is about telling those two places apart.

After the verb, nothing happens. When the adjective comes after ist, sind or wird, it is completely bare — no ending, ever, for any gender or number: Das Auto ist neu. Die Wohnung ist neu. Die Autos sind neu. This half is free, and it works just like Turkish and English.

In front of a noun, an ending is compulsory. There is no such thing as a bare adjective standing before a German noun. das neue Auto, ein neues Auto, mit neuen Autos. Leaving the ending off entirely is more noticeable to German ears than picking the wrong one, so when in doubt, add something.

Here is the idea that makes the famous table manageable. Every German noun phrase has to show two things somewhere: its gender (is it a der, die or das word) and its case — the job the noun is doing in the sentence. Somebody has to do that work. If the article in front already does it clearly, the adjective can be lazy and just takes -e or -en. If there is no article, or the article is vague, the adjective has to do the job itself and takes the ending der/die/das would have had. That is the entire logic behind all three tables.

So, three situations. After der/die/das: only two endings exist in the whole table, -e and -en — -e in the nominative singular corner, -en everywhere else. After ein/kein/mein: the same, except in the three spots where ein itself shows nothing (ein looks identical for a der-word and a das-word), and there the adjective steps in: ein guter Kaffee, ein neues Auto. With no article at all: guter Kaffee, kalte Milch, kaltes Wasser — the adjective simply wears der/die/das's own ending. And one cheat that is right far more often than it deserves to be: if you are not in the nominative singular, guess -en.

lessons.title: bigger, biggest — comparison
lessons.summary: Add -er to compare two things and am -sten for the winner — then learn the five irregulars and stop mixing up als and wie.
lessons.rule:
An adjective is a describing word: big, old, cheap. When you hold two things next to each other you need a stronger version of it — bigger, older, cheaper. That stronger version has a name: the comparative. And when one thing beats everything else you need the top version — biggest, oldest — called the superlative. German builds both almost exactly the way English does with short words, so this lesson is mostly good news.

Comparing two things: add -er. klein → kleiner, schnell → schneller, billig → billiger. German does this to every adjective, no matter how long it is. English gives up on long words and switches to more (more interesting), and Turkish puts daha in front. German never does either. It is interessanter, wichtiger, bequemer — never mehr interessant.

The winner: am plus -sten. am kleinsten, am schnellsten, am billigsten. Two small adjustments. If the adjective ends in d, t, s, z or ß, an extra e slides in so your mouth can manage it: alt → am ältesten, kurz → am kürzesten. And many short one-syllable adjectives grow an Umlaut — the two dots — as soon as they are compared: alt → älter, jung → jünger, lang → länger, warm → wärmer. There is no rule for which ones do this. It is a small memorised group, and the second table below is most of it.

Now the part people get wrong for years: wie or als? If the two things are equal, use the pair so … wie: Ich bin so groß wie du. If one is more than the other, use als: Ich bin größer als du. The test is mechanical — the moment there is an -er form in the sentence, the next little word is als. You will hear people in Berlin say größer wie du; it is still marked wrong in writing and in every exam, so do not copy it.

One more thing you will see everywhere. Next to am besten there is a second superlative that stands directly in front of a noun and takes an ending: der beste Kaffee, die größte Stadt, mein bester Freund. Same meaning, different position. Use am …sten after a verb, and der/die/das …ste in front of a noun.

lessons.title: sich freuen, sich waschen — reflexive verbs
lessons.summary: Some German verbs need a small extra word pointing back at the doer — and the ones English leaves unmarked are exactly the ones you will forget.
lessons.rule:
Usually an action goes out from you and lands on something else: Ich wasche das Auto. Sometimes it loops back and lands on you: Ich wasche mich. — I wash myself. That little word pointing back at the doer is called a reflexive pronoun, and a verb that needs one is a reflexive verb. Turkish handles this inside the verb itself (yıkanmak); German uses a separate word that you must remember to say out loud.

In a dictionary these verbs are listed with sich stuck to the front — sich waschen, sich freuen. Treat that sich the way you treat der, die and das on a noun: it is part of the word, learn them together. In a real sentence the sich changes to match whoever is doing it, and it sits right after the conjugated verb: Ich freue mich. Heute freue ich mich. Freust du dich? Only ich and du have two different shapes to worry about; everybody else uses sich, uns or euch for both jobs.

Which shape — mich or mir? Two of German's grammar jobs are involved. The accusative is the thing the action lands on directly. The dative is the person the action is done for or to. So: Ich wasche mich. — nothing else is being washed, only me, so the accusative mich. But Ich wasche mir die Hände. — now die Hände is the thing being washed, so I step back into the dative mir, meaning for myself. The rule in practice: if a second thing appears after the pronoun, switch to the dative. Same with Ich putze mir die Zähne. and Ich ziehe mir eine Jacke an.

The real trap is not the endings. It is the verbs that carry a pronoun in German while English says nothing at all, so you will simply leave it out. Learn these as fixed phrases:

  • sich freuen — to be glad, to look forward to
  • sich erinnern an — to remember
  • sich beeilen — to hurry
  • sich entschuldigen — to apologise
  • sich vorstellen — to introduce yourself
  • sich setzen — to sit down
  • sich fühlen — to feel
  • sich interessieren für — to be interested in

Two practical notes. sich vorstellen means two different things depending on the shape: Ich stelle mich vor is I introduce myself, while Ich stelle mir das vor is I imagine that. And you will hear the polite version constantly in Germany — Setzen Sie sich, bitte. at the doctor, Beeilen Sie sich! on a platform. With Sie the pronoun is always sich, with a small s.

lessons.title: Telling someone what to do
lessons.summary: Three command forms for three kinds of you — and the polite one is what you will actually hear on the train, at the doctor and at the Amt.
lessons.rule:
An imperative is the form you use to tell or ask somebody to do something: Come in. Wait here. Sign there. German has three of them, because German has three words for you: du for one person you know, ihr for several people you know, and Sie for strangers, officials and anyone you have not been invited to call du.

The du command. Take the ordinary du form and chop off the -st: du gehst → Geh!, du kommst → Komm!, du machst → Mach!. And leave the word du out — the command carries no pronoun. Two details. If the stem ends in t or d, keep an -e so it is sayable: Warte!, Arbeite!. And if the du form changes its vowel from e to i, the command keeps that change: du nimmst → Nimm!, du gibst → Gib!, du sprichst → Sprich!, du liest → Lies!. But if the change was a to ä, the command throws the dots away again: du fährst → Fahr!, du schläfst → Schlaf!

The ihr command is the easy one: it is exactly the normal ihr form with the pronoun removed. Geht! Kommt! Wartet! Nehmt! The Sie command is also simple, and it is the only one that keeps its pronoun: the full -en verb, then Sie. Gehen Sie! Kommen Sie! Warten Sie! It looks identical to a statement with the words flipped, and that is all it is.

sein is the one genuinely irregular verb here: Sei ruhig!, Seid ruhig!, Seien Sie ruhig! — never Sind Sie. And a separable verb splits as usual, with its little front piece dropping to the end of the sentence: Steh bitte auf!, Macht die Tür zu!, Steigen Sie bitte ein!

One social point that matters more than the grammar. A bare command sounds sharp in German, so bitte goes in almost every one: Komm bitte um acht., Warten Sie bitte einen Moment. You will meet the Sie form constantly — Nehmen Sie bitte Platz. at the doctor, Steigen Sie bitte ein. on a platform, Füllen Sie das Formular aus. at the Amt. On written signs German often skips the imperative entirely and uses the plain dictionary form instead: Bitte nicht rauchen., Tür schließen., Drücken, Ziehen. Same meaning, no ending to worry about.

lessons.title: Saying when: time, manner, place
lessons.summary: German puts time before place — the exact opposite of English — and chooses between am, im, um and no preposition at all.
lessons.rule:
A German sentence has one hard rule you already know: the verb sits in second position. Everything else — when, why, how, where — comes after it, and it comes in a fixed order. That order is this whole lesson. Germans remember it as TeKaMoLo:

  • Te = temporal — when? morgen, um acht Uhr, jeden Tag
  • Ka = kausal — why? wegen der Arbeit
  • Mo = modal — how? mit dem Zug, zu Fuß, allein
  • Lo = lokal — where? nach Berlin, ins Büro

So: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin. — when, how, where. English says exactly the same thing in almost the opposite order: I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow — where, how, when. That reversal is why the time keeps sliding to the end of your German sentences for months. Burn in the short version: time first, place last. You will rarely need all four slots at once — two is normal, three is a long sentence.

You can also lift the time expression to the very front, and Germans do this constantly: Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. But the verb still has to be the second element, so the subject jumps behind it. Morgen fahre ich — never Morgen ich fahre. The rest of the order (how, then where) stays exactly as it was.

Which little word goes in front of the time? Three of them cover nearly everything. um for clock times: um 8 Uhr. am for days, dates and parts of the day: am Montag, am Wochenende, am Abend, am 3. Mai. im for months and seasons: im Januar, im Sommer. One oddity to memorise on its own: it is in der Nacht, not am.

And sometimes you use no preposition at all. Anything built with next, last or every stands completely bare: nächste Woche, letzten Monat, jeden Tag, jeden Morgen. So do heute, morgen and gestern. Turkish marks this with an ending and English adds on or in, so your instinct will be to put something there. Resist it — in nächster Woche is wrong, it is simply nächste Woche.

lessons.title: Numbers, telling the time, and dates
lessons.summary: German says numbers backwards above twenty, uses the 24-hour clock officially, and halb drei means 2:30 — not 3:30.
lessons.rule:
Up to twelve you simply memorise: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you glue the digit onto zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn — but sechzehn and siebzehn quietly drop a letter, and so do sechzig and siebzig.

Then German goes backwards. From 21 upwards the small digit is said first, joined by und, and the whole thing is written as one word: einundzwanzig is literally one-and-twenty. 47 is siebenundvierzig — seven-and-forty. Hundreds go in front as normal: 134 is hundertvierunddreißig.

This is not a cute quirk, it is a daily problem. Someone reads you a phone number or an account number and you write 72 where they said 27, because the zwei arrived first. Prices too: 3,50 € is said drei Euro fünfzig — and note the comma. German uses a comma where English uses a decimal point, and a dot where English uses a thousands comma, so 1.500 means one thousand five hundred.

The clock. Timetables, appointments, opening hours and anything official use the 24-hour clock: Der Zug fährt um 14:32 Uhr, spoken vierzehn Uhr zweiunddreißig. In casual speech people use 1 to 12 — and here is the trap that catches everyone: halb drei means 2:30, not 3:30. German halb looks forward: half-way to three. So 7:30 is halb acht. The rule of thumb is add one to the English hour.

The rest is friendly: Viertel nach drei is 3:15, Viertel vor drei is 2:45, zehn nach vier is 4:10, zwanzig vor fünf is 4:40. (In eastern and southern Germany you will also hear viertel drei for 2:15 — just know it exists.) Dates run day.month.year: 03.08.2026 is 3 August 2026, so an American-style 08.03 would be read as 8 March. The dot after a number means 3rd, and am 3. Mai is spoken am dritten Mai.

drills.explain: Five-and-forty, in that order and as one word with no spaces.

lessons.title: es gibt and man — two phrases you need constantly
lessons.summary: es gibt means there is / there are and always takes the accusative; man means people in general and takes the er/sie/es verb form.
lessons.rule:
es gibt is how German says there is and there are. Word for word it means it gives, which is useless as a translation — so learn it as one frozen block and stop taking it apart.

Two facts about it, and neither ever changes. First, the form is always es gibt, even when you are talking about a hundred things. Es gibt einen Supermarkt. Es gibt viele Leute. Never es geben, never sie gibt — the subject of the sentence is that little es, not the things that exist.

Second, what follows it is in the accusative. The accusative is the form a noun takes when it is the thing a verb acts on — I see the man, I buy a coffee. In practice only masculine words visibly change, and they change like this: ein → einen, der → den, kein → keinen. So Es gibt einen Supermarkt, but Es gibt eine Apotheke (feminine) and Es gibt ein Problem (neuter) with no change at all. Questions behave the same: Gibt es hier einen Bahnhof?

The second phrase is man. It means one / you / people in general — nobody specific. English has one, but it sounds so formal that people avoid it; German man is completely ordinary and you will meet it every day, above all in rules and on signs: Hier darf man nicht parken. Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch? In Deutschland bezahlt man oft bar.

Two things to keep straight. man always takes the same verb form as er/sie/es: man sagt, man kann, man darf — never man sagen. And man (one n, small m) is not der Mann (two n, capital M, an adult male). They sound identical out loud, so only context tells them apart — but in writing the difference is visible and getting it wrong is noticed.

lessons.title: würde, hätte, könnte — being polite and hypothetical
lessons.summary: The umlaut forms that turn a demand into a request. This is how you order food, ask a stranger for help, and say no without sounding rude.
lessons.rule:
German verbs have a second, softer gear. Next to the everyday forms you already know — ich habe, ich bin, ich kann — sits a polite twin with an umlaut in it: ich hätte, ich wäre, ich könnte. Textbooks call this Konjunktiv II. Forget the name. Think of it as the please gear.

This is not decoration, and it is not optional. In a German bakery or at the Bürgeramt, the plain present tense lands like an order. Ich will einen Kaffee is grammatically perfect and socially rude — it comes out roughly as Give me a coffee. What people actually say, hundreds of times a day, is Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. Same when you stop a stranger: Können Sie mir helfen? is fine with a colleague, but Könnten Sie mir helfen? is what you say to someone you have never met. The difference is two dots and a t, and Germans hear it immediately.

Six words do almost all the work, and you can learn them as vocabulary rather than as grammar:

  • ich hätte — I'd like / I'd have, the ordering word
  • ich wäre — I would be
  • ich könnte — I could, and könnten Sie for requests
  • ich müsste — I'd have to, for softening bad news
  • ich sollte — I should
  • ich würde — I would, the all-purpose one

For every other verb you do not need a special form at all. Take würde and park the infinitive — the dictionary form of the verb, the one ending in -en — at the very end of the sentence: Ich würde gern einen Termin machen. That is the same shape you already use with können and müssen: one verb in second position, the other waiting at the end.

Two things to guard. haben and sein keep their own forms and never take würde — say Das wäre gut, not das würde gut sein. And watch the umlaut, because it carries the entire meaning: ich hatte is the past (I had), ich hätte is the polite one. The same gear also handles things that are not real: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich mehr lernen.

helfen sends its person into the dative, so it is mir, never mich.
Sie takes the -en ending: hätten. Haben Sie morgen Zeit? is not wrong, just harder-edged.
wäre, not würde sein. sein has its own polite form.

The two dots are the whole message. hatte is the past tense — you just said you used to enjoy coffee. hätte is the polite request.

lessons.title: werden + participle — the passive
lessons.summary: How official German says that something gets done without naming who does it — and how to tell that apart from a plain description.
lessons.rule:
A past participle is the verb form you already use for the past: gemacht, gekauft, gebaut, bezahlt, geschlossen. It usually starts with ge- and it never changes its shape. Keep it in mind, because this whole lesson is werden plus one of those.

A normal sentence names a doer: Der Mann füllt das Formular aus. But official German — letters from the Amt, signs, rental contracts, instructions — usually does not care who does it. So it flips the sentence: the thing becomes the topic and the doer vanishes completely. Das Formular wird ausgefüllt. Grammar books call this the passive. Turkish does the same job with a suffix inside the verb; German does it with two words that wrap around the sentence.

The shape is always the same. werden takes the normal verb slot (second thing in the sentence) and changes to match the subject — wird for one thing, werden for several. The participle falls to the very last position and just sits there. Everything else — times, places, nicht — goes in the middle: Der Brief wird heute nicht geschickt.

Two traps. First, werden on its own means to become: Ich werde müde is I'm getting tired. It only builds a passive when a participle is waiting at the end. Second, sein + participle looks similar but says something different: it describes a state, not an action. Das Geschäft wird um 20 Uhr geschlossen means somebody closes it at eight. Das Geschäft ist geschlossen means it is shut right now.

German can even build a passive with no subject at all, which English simply cannot do. Hier wird gebaut on a fence means building work going on here. Heute wird nicht gearbeitet means nobody is working today. You will meet these constantly on signs and in letters. Reading them correctly matters far more than producing them — so aim to recognise the pattern instantly, and keep writing your own sentences in the normal active way.

lessons.title: damit, dafür, worauf — the da-/wo- compounds
lessons.summary: German fuses a small word and a thing into one word — damit, dafür, darauf — and never leaves the preposition dangling at the end of a question.
lessons.rule:
A preposition is one of those small positioning words: mit, für, auf, an, über, von, zu. In English you can put it straight after one — with it, for it, about it. German cannot. There is no such thing as mit es or für es. Instead the two ideas fuse into a single word.

The recipe is da + the preposition. mit dem Auto becomes damit, für das Zimmer becomes dafür, von dem Film becomes davon, nach dem Essen becomes danach. If the preposition starts with a vowel, an -r- slides in to keep it pronounceable: da + auf → darauf, da + an → daran, da + über → darüber, da + in → darin. Nobody says daauf. That extra r has no meaning at all — it is purely so your mouth can get through the word.

Questions work exactly the same way, with wo instead of da: womit, wofür, wovon, and with the same -r- before a vowel: worauf, woran, worüber. Here English will actively mislead you. English strands the preposition at the end — What are you waiting for? — and German never does that. It fuses the two into one word and puts it at the front: Worauf wartest du?

One sentence decides which route you take: things get a da-/wo- word, people never do. People keep the plain preposition plus a normal pronoun. So Ich fahre mit dem Bus → Ich fahre damit, but Ich fahre mit Anna → Ich fahre mit ihr. And the questions split the same way: Womit fährst du? for a thing, Mit wem fährst du? for a person.

These matter more than they look. Lots of German verbs come glued to a preposition — warten auf, denken an, sprechen über, sich freuen auf — and the moment someone refers back to the thing, out comes darauf, daran, darüber. A last warning: damit also exists as a completely different word meaning so that, as in Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich hier arbeiten kann. Same spelling, different job — the comma in front of it gives it away.

examples.de: Fährst du mit dem Bus? — Ja, ich fahre damit.
examples.en: Do you go by bus? — Yes, I go by it.

examples.en: I've been waiting for it for a long time.
examples.note: warten goes with auf, and auf starts with a vowel, so the -r- slides in: darauf.
English hangs the for on the end; German fuses it onto wo and puts the whole thing first.

examples.de: Ich fahre mit Anna. Ich fahre mit ihr.
examples.en: I'm going with Anna. I'm going with her.
examples.note: A person, so no fusion at all — plain preposition plus the normal pronoun.

The standard way to agree in a meeting. Its opposite is Ich bin dagegen.

Same fusion rule, plus the extra -r- because auf begins with a vowel. daauf is unpronounceable, so darauf it is.
English leaves the preposition at the end of the question; German never does. It joins wo and auf into one word at the front.
